entries.what_happened: The manuscript 'The crossing number of complete bipartite graphs' (build/paper.tex, dated 23 September 2026) claims Theorem 1: for all positive integers m and n, cr(Kₘ,ₙ) = dₘ dₙ, where dᵣ = ⌊r/2⌋⌊(r−1)/2⌋. This is exactly the Zarankiewicz number Z(m,n) of the list. Upper bound: the classical axis drawing (one vertex class on a vertical axis, the other on a horizontal axis, straight edges, positions chosen generically to avoid triple concurrences) has dₘ dₙ crossings; the count is written out. Lower bound: for odd n = 2s+1 with m ≥ 3, take a minimum drawing with no crossings between edges sharing an endpoint. Its signed-intersection matrix J satisfies zᵀJy = 0 for every pair of cycles (Lemma 'Cycle pairing'). A polynomial rank detector Φ built from Lagrange weights makes the off-diagonal blocks have rank at most the crossing count between two stars. A subspace-intersection inequality, Σᵢ,ⱼ dim(Uᵢ∩Vⱼ) ≤ ⌊m²/4⌋N, which the text proves, then gives a sum over ordered pairs i ≠ k of ranks of at least 2dₘ dₙ. Each crossing is counted twice, so c(D) ≥ dₘ dₙ. For even n, deleting each second-class vertex in turn gives (n−2)c(D) ≥ n dₘ dₙ₋₁ = (n−2)dₘ dₙ. The cases m ≤ 2 or n ≤ 2 are zero by nonnegativity. The other manuscript in the family, 'The crossing number of complete graphs', concerns Kₙ only and is not used for this match.
entries.delivers: For every pair of positive integers m, n, the claim gives cr(Kₘ,ₙ) = Z(m,n), so no drawing of Kₘ,ₙ in the manuscript's class has fewer crossings than Z(m,n). This is the 'no' answer to the list's question. It covers all pairs (m,n), as the list's part (i) requires, and it includes the lower bound the list identifies as open. The class is restricted. A drawing has distinct vertex points and each edge is a simple continuous arc avoiding the vertices. Edge interiors meet in finitely many proper crossings (locally two arcs crossing transversally), with no tangencies, overlaps, triple points or common subarcs. Crossings are counted as points, so repeated crossings of one edge pair each count. Within that class there is no restriction on vertex positions or edge routes. The abstract says the result resolves Turán's brickyard problem. The manuscript does not restate the list's yes/no question, but its theorem is the two-sided equality over all (m,n) that answers it.
entries.remains: If the claim holds, nothing is left open for Kₘ,ₙ within the manuscript's class. Outside that class the manuscript says nothing. Drawings with tangential contacts, triple points, infinitely many intersection points, or other crossing conventions (counting crossing pairs, or only odd crossings, which the introduction distinguishes) are not addressed.
entries.direction: proves the Zarankiewicz formula for all Kₘ,ₙ, answering Turán's question 'no' (no drawing beats Z(m,n))
entries.object: No counterexample is constructed, since none exists under the claim. The only explicit drawing is the classical axis drawing, which gives the upper bound dₘ dₙ. Its vertex positions are chosen by a genericity argument, not written out.
entries.doubts: The lower bound rests on the cycle-pairing identity. Its proof handles edges shared by the two cycles through a prose description of shifted tracks in crossing and bend disks, supported by figures. The claims that a common small shift creates no new intersections and that seam contributions cancel are asserted in words, not checked in formulas. The manuscript flags no step as sketched and states no hedge. The abstract and Theorem 1 agree.

entries.not_relevant_because: The manuscripts concern crossing numbers of complete bipartite graphs drawn in the plane, not the extremal function z(m,n;s,t). Neither states, bounds or uses the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with no Kₛ,ₜ, and neither gives any asymptotic for z(n,n;s,t). The shared name belongs to Zarankiewicz's crossing-number conjecture, a different problem, as the matching pass itself noted. The dimension-counting lemmas in the bipartite manuscript do not concern forbidden subgraphs.

The manuscripts determine cr(Kₙ) = Z(n) for complete graphs and cr(Kₘ,ₙ) for complete bipartite graphs, and they claim nothing about cr(G) for any other graph G. Albertson's conjecture is the inequality cr(G) ≥ cr(Kχ(G)) over all finite graphs. The only instances the family covers are G = Kᵣ, where the inequality is an equality, so the family does not bear on the inequality. The matching pass's link runs through the value cr(Kᵣ) on the right-hand side, which the problem does not ask for. The complete-graph manuscript states its cycle-pairing lemma for every finite simple graph, but uses it only to bound crossings of complete graphs.
